title: Chemical variables predicting colonization risk of the invasive New Zealand mudsnail (Potamopyrgus antipodarum) in Pennsylvania’s flowing waters
content:
Abstract

As costs and efforts associated with control of invasive species are often significant, data on habitat variables associated with colonization potential are needed to prioritize and target areas for prevention efforts prior to introduction. Recently, invasive New Zealand Mudsnails (Potamopyrgus antipodarum; NZMS) have undergone significant range expansions in parts of the Mid-Atlantic United States such as Pennsylvania. However, data on chemical parameters in flowing waters at risk of colonization by NZMS are largely lacking for this region. We compiled a dataset of over 400 survey sites for NZMS throughout Pennsylvania and used available water chemistry data on 57 chemical parameters for a subset of these sites to evaluate parameter-specific chemical sensitivity associated with occurrence of NZMS. We found significant associations among NZMS and chemical variables such as alkalinity, hardness, calcium, nutrients, specific conductance, bromide, osmotic pressure, strontium, and sulfate. Chemical sensitivity results were used to create a statewide chemical suitability model, which suggests several regions in Pennsylvania are at high risk for NZMS colonization. Parameters in high-risk waters are likely attributable to factors such as agriculture, urbanization, and karst geology. This model is intended as a tool for prioritizing prevention efforts and monitoring in Pennsylvania streams and rivers. Resource agencies and partners could use our study and model as a template to predict colonization risk of NZMS or other invasive aquatic mollusks in other regions.
